variables.notes: Scope and global variables are B05 scope. a, b = b, a is used in swap_values as a preview; tuple unpacking proper is B06 unpacking. Names-as-references for mutable objects (aliasing) is B06 mutability_aliasing. naming_rules covers the PEP 8 naming conventions B01 deferred here; it is core, so pep8_style.spacing_and_layout (non-core) is neither a prerequisite nor encompassed.

data_types.notes: Only two topics because the type-specific material is owned by integers_floats, booleans, none_type and type_conversion in this batch, and strings by B03. isinstance() and classes-as-types belong to the OOP batch (B11). D2 previews "2" + "3" joining strings; B03 string_concatenation owns concatenation and should encompass data_types.types_decide_operations.

integers_floats.notes: round() and abs() are taught here because floats need them early; B05 builtin_functions should reference rather than re-teach them. Binary representation, epsilon methods and the decimal module are B14 floating_point_precision; math module functions are B13 math_module.

arithmetic_operators.notes: Augmented assignment (+= etc.) is owned by variables.update_with_own_value. Divisibility tests with if are B04 conditionals, which should encompass modulo_patterns. ^ is mentioned only as 'not power'; bitwise operators are B14 binary_bitwise.

expressions.notes: print(2 + 3) vs print('2 + 3') (deferred from B01 print_output) is expressions.evaluate_expressions KP1. Conditional expressions (x if c else y) are B04.

constants.notes: Global constants used inside functions belong to B05 scope; math.pi etc. to B13 math_module; Enum to B11 enums.

none_type.notes: Functions that return None implicitly (and print() returning None) belong to B05 return_values, which should encompass none_type.none_value. 'is' vs '==' on mutable objects belongs to B06 mutability_aliasing; check_for_none only covers None and the literal warning.

type_conversion.notes: bool() conversion is booleans.truthiness. Handling ValueError with try/except is B09 exceptions (cs50p 'get an integer' function). str() for building output with + is B03 string_concatenation, which should encompass type_conversion.numbers_and_strings. list()/tuple()/set() conversions belong to B06/B07.

user_input.notes: The concept graph says user_input comes before variables; here it comes after, since storing the answer needs assignment. Re-prompting until valid input is B04 while_loops (sentinel) and B09 exceptions. Input methods like .strip()/.lower() on answers are B03 string_methods.

booleans.notes: Using truthiness in if/while (if name:) is B04 conditionals; summing booleans to count is B04 loop_patterns / B05 builtin_functions.

comparison_operators.notes: String comparison is owned here; B03 should only add case-insensitive comparison via .lower(). The membership operator in is B03 strings / B06 lists. math.isclose is B13 math_module.

logical_operators.notes: All examples are standalone expressions; B04 conditionals uses them in if/while and should encompass logical_operators.and_or_not and combine_conditions.

topics.title: Storing a value in a variable
topics.summary: Assign a value to a name with =, use the name to get the value back, and recognise the NameError from using a name that was never assigned.

knowledge_points.title: Assign a value, then use the name
knowledge_points.worked_example:
age = 36
print(age)
# 36
= stores the value on the right under the name on the left.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what a short program prints; write the assignment that makes a given print show a target value.

knowledge_points.title: A name vs text in quotes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
city = "Lima"
print(city)
print("city")
# Lima
# city
Without quotes Python looks up the variable; with quotes it is just text.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output of look-alike pairs with and without quotes; fix a print that shows the name instead of the value.

knowledge_points.title: Using a name before assigning it is a NameError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(score)
score = 10
# NameError: name 'score' is not defined
The assignment must run before the line that uses it.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which programs run and which stop with NameError; reorder lines (Parsons) so the program works.

knowledge_points.title: Names are case-sensitive and must be spelled exactly
knowledge_points.worked_example:
total = 5
print(Total)
# NameError: Total and total are different names
knowledge_points.practice: Find the misspelled or wrongly capitalised name in short programs and fix it.

topics.title: Reassigning variables and tracing their values
topics.summary: Predict a variable's value after several assignments, including copying one variable into another, using a trace table.

knowledge_points.title: Reassignment replaces the old value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 5
x = 8
print(x)
# 8
A variable holds one value at a time; the 5 is gone.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the printed value after two or three assignments to the same name.

knowledge_points.title: Order matters: a print shows the value at that moment
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 5
print(x)
x = 8
print(x)
# 5
# 8
knowledge_points.practice: Predict multi-line output where prints and reassignments are interleaved.

knowledge_points.title: b = a copies the current value; later changes to a do not affect b
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = 3
b = a
a = 10
print(a, b)
# 10 3
knowledge_points.practice: Predict both values after copy-then-reassign sequences; multiple choice designed around the 'b follows a' misconception.

knowledge_points.title: Tracing several variables with a table
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in a trace table for 4-6 assignments across two or three variables.

topics.title: Updating a variable from its own value
topics.summary: Use x = x + 1 and the augmented operators +=, -=, *= to update counters and running totals, and avoid updating a variable that was never initialised.

knowledge_points.title: x = x + 1: the right side uses the old value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
count = 4
count = count + 1
print(count)
# 5
Python evaluates count + 1 first (4 + 1), then stores 5 in count.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict values after one or two self-updates; trace a sequence of updates.

knowledge_points.title: Shorthand: +=, -=, *=, /=
knowledge_points.worked_example:
score = 10
score += 5   # same as score = score + 5
score -= 3
print(score)
# 12
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite long-form updates with augmented operators; predict the result of a mixed sequence.

knowledge_points.title: A running total over several steps
knowledge_points.worked_example:
total = 0
total += 4
total += 7
total += 2
print(total)
# 13
Start at 0, then add each amount.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the lines that total a shopping list of given prices; fill a trace table for the total.

knowledge_points.title: Common bugs: no starting value, and an update that is never stored
knowledge_points.worked_example:
count += 1      # NameError: count was never assigned
x = 5
x + 1           # computed, then thrown away
print(x)        # still 5
knowledge_points.practice: Spot why each program fails or prints the wrong value; fix it.

topics.title: Swapping the values of two variables
topics.summary: Swap two variables correctly with a temporary variable or a, b = b, a, and explain why the naive two-line swap loses a value.

knowledge_points.title: The naive swap loses a value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = 1
b = 2
a = b
b = a
print(a, b)
# 2 2  (the original 1 was overwritten)
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the naive swap; predict the output.

knowledge_points.title: Swap with a temporary variable
knowledge_points.worked_example:
temp = a
a = b
b = temp
The temp keeps a's old value safe while a is overwritten.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the three swap lines (Parsons); fix a temp swap with two lines in the wrong order.

knowledge_points.title: Python's one-line swap
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a, b = b, a
The right side is evaluated fully first, then both names are assigned. (Unpacking is explained fully later.)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict values after one-line swaps; replace a temp swap with the one-liner.

knowledge_points.title: Rotating three values
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x, y, z = 1, 2, 3
x, y, z = y, z, x
print(x, y, z)
# 2 3 1
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of a three-way rotation; write a rotation that produces a target order.

topics.title: Naming variables: rules and conventions
topics.summary: Choose names that are legal (letters, digits, underscores, not starting with a digit, not a keyword), do not shadow built-ins like print, and follow PEP 8's descriptive snake_case.

knowledge_points.title: What makes a name legal
knowledge_points.worked_example:
user_age = 30    # ok
_count = 0       # ok
2nd_place = 1    # SyntaxError: cannot start with a digit
first-name = 1   # SyntaxError: - is minus
knowledge_points.practice: Classify a list of names as legal or illegal; fix illegal names.

knowledge_points.title: Keywords cannot be names; built-in names should not be
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class = 3       # SyntaxError: class is a keyword
print = 5
print("hi")     # TypeError: print is now the number 5
knowledge_points.practice: Pick which names are keywords; explain (multiple choice) why a program broke after assigning to print or input.

knowledge_points.title: PEP 8: lower_snake_case
knowledge_points.worked_example:
totalPrice = 5   # works, but not Python style
total_price = 5  # PEP 8
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the PEP 8 name among options; rename variables in a short program.

knowledge_points.title: Descriptive names make code readable
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 60 * 24        # what is x?
minutes_per_day = 60 * 24
Prefer names that say what the value means; single letters only for short-lived values.
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the best name for a described value; rename vague variables in a 4-line program.

topics.title: Every value has a type
topics.summary: Name the type of int, float, str and bool values, check it with type(), and explain that a variable's type is the type of the value it currently holds.

knowledge_points.title: Four basic types and type()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(type(42))      # <class 'int'>
print(type(3.5))     # <class 'float'>
print(type("hi"))    # <class 'str'>
print(type(True))    # <class 'bool'>
knowledge_points.practice: Predict type() for literals; match values to their type names.

knowledge_points.title: Quotes make a string, even around digits
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(type("42"))   # <class 'str'>
print(type(42))     # <class 'int'>
print("42", 42)     # 42 42  (they print the same)
knowledge_points.practice: Classify look-alike values ("42", 42, "4.2", 4.2, "True", True) by type.

knowledge_points.title: A variable's type follows its current value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 7
print(type(x))   # <class 'int'>
x = "seven"
print(type(x))   # <class 'str'>
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the type after each reassignment in a short program; trace types in a table.

topics.title: Types decide what operators do
topics.summary: Predict whether an operation works by looking at the types involved: + adds numbers but joins strings, and mixing a string with a number raises TypeError.

knowledge_points.title: Same operator, different types
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(2 + 3)       # 5
print("2" + "3")   # 23
On numbers + adds; on strings it joins the text.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict outputs for + on pairs of numbers and pairs of strings.

knowledge_points.title: A string plus a number is a TypeError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("2" + 3)
# TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
Python will not guess whether you meant 5 or "23".
knowledge_points.practice: For each expression decide: value or TypeError; give the value where there is one.

knowledge_points.title: Finding where a value got the wrong type
knowledge_points.worked_example:
price = "5"       # quotes: this is a str
total = price + 1   # TypeError on this line
The error appears where the value is used, but the bug is where it was created.
knowledge_points.practice: Locate and fix the line that gave a variable the wrong type.

topics.title: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing
topics.summary: Compute with + - * and /, knowing that / always gives a float and that dividing by zero is an error.

knowledge_points.title: +, - and * on numbers
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(7 + 5)   # 12
print(7 - 5)   # 2
print(7 * 5)   # 35
* is multiplication (not x).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results; write the expression for a word problem.

knowledge_points.title: / always gives a float
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(6 / 3)   # 2.0
print(7 / 2)   # 3.5
Even when it divides exactly, / gives a decimal result.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of divisions, including exact ones; multiple choice between 2 and 2.0.

knowledge_points.title: Arithmetic with variables
knowledge_points.worked_example:
price = 4
qty = 3
cost = price * qty
print(cost)   # 12
knowledge_points.practice: Write the line that computes a result from given variables; predict output.

knowledge_points.title: Dividing by zero is an error
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(5 / 0)
# ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which lines raise ZeroDivisionError (including via a variable that is 0).

topics.title: Floor division // and remainder %
topics.summary: Use // for the whole-number quotient and % for the remainder, convert units such as minutes to hours and minutes, and predict results with negative numbers.

knowledge_points.title: // gives the whole number of times
knowledge_points.practice: Predict // results for ints and floats.

knowledge_points.title: % gives the remainder
knowledge_points.practice: Predict remainders, including when the left number is smaller.

knowledge_points.title: Using // and % together to convert units
knowledge_points.worked_example:
minutes = 135
print(minutes // 60, minutes % 60)
# 2 15  (2 hours 15 minutes)
knowledge_points.practice: Write code that converts seconds into minutes and seconds, or cents into euros and cents.

knowledge_points.title: Negative numbers: // rounds down
knowledge_points.practice: Predict // and % with one negative operand.

topics.title: Patterns with %: even/odd, digits and wrap-around
topics.summary: Apply % and // to classic problems: test even/odd, extract the last digit, and wrap a value around a cycle such as hours on a clock.

knowledge_points.title: Even or odd with % 2
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(14 % 2)   # 0 -> even
print(9 % 2)    # 1 -> odd
knowledge_points.practice: Predict n % 2 for several numbers; say which are even.

knowledge_points.title: Last digit with % 10, dropping it with // 10
knowledge_points.practice: Predict last digits and shortened numbers; write code printing the tens digit.

knowledge_points.title: Wrapping around a cycle
knowledge_points.worked_example:
hour = 22
print((hour + 5) % 24)   # 3
The % keeps the result inside 0-23.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute clock times and weekdays after adding hours or days; fix a version that forgets the % and prints 27.

topics.title: Powers with **
topics.summary: Raise numbers to powers with **, take square roots with ** 0.5, and know that ^ is not the power operator.

knowledge_points.title: ** raises to a power
knowledge_points.practice: Predict powers; write the expression for the area of a square of side s.

knowledge_points.title: ^ is not power
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(2 ^ 3)    # 1  (a different operator)
print(2 ** 3)   # 8
Use ** for powers.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix formulas that used ^; multiple choice on which expression computes 2 cubed.

knowledge_points.title: Roots and negative powers give floats
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of fractional and negative exponents; write a square-root expression.

knowledge_points.title: Integers can be as big as you like
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(2 ** 100)
# 1267650600228229401496703205376
Python ints never overflow; they are exact.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether a huge power prints exactly or as a float (int vs float base).

topics.title: Integers and floats
topics.summary: Tell int from float values, predict when a result becomes a float, and read large and very small numbers written with underscores or e-notation.

knowledge_points.title: 7 and 7.0 are different types
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(type(7))     # <class 'int'>
print(type(7.0))   # <class 'float'>
print(7 == 7.0)    # True: same value
knowledge_points.practice: Classify values as int or float; predict type() results.

knowledge_points.title: Mixing int and float gives a float
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(2 + 0.5)    # 2.5
print(3 * 1.0)    # 3.0
print(8 / 4)      # 2.0  (/ is always float)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the value and type of mixed expressions.

knowledge_points.title: Writing large numbers with underscores
knowledge_points.worked_example:
population = 8_100_000_000
print(population)   # 8100000000
Underscores are ignored; commas would make several values.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a number written with commas; predict printed values of underscore literals.

knowledge_points.title: Scientific notation: e means times ten to the power
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(1.5e3)       # 1500.0
print(0.00001)      # 1e-05
Very large or small floats print in e-notation.
knowledge_points.practice: Convert between e-notation and ordinary decimals; predict how a value prints.

topics.title: Rounding and float surprises
topics.summary: Expect small errors in float arithmetic, round results with round(x) and round(x, n), and use abs() for distances.

knowledge_points.title: Floats are approximations
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(0.1 + 0.2)
# 0.30000000000000004
Most decimals cannot be stored exactly in binary, so tiny errors appear.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which sums print exactly and which show a tiny error (multiple choice); explain the cause.

knowledge_points.title: round(x) to the nearest whole number; ties go to the even neighbour
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(round(3.7))   # 4
print(round(2.5))   # 2
print(round(3.5))   # 4
knowledge_points.practice: Predict round() results, including .5 cases.

knowledge_points.title: round(x, n) for n decimal places
knowledge_points.practice: Write expressions that round prices and averages for display; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: abs() for size and distance
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(abs(-3.5))       # 3.5
print(abs(4 - 10))     # 6: how far apart 4 and 10 are
knowledge_points.practice: Write the distance between two variables; predict abs() results.

topics.title: Expressions produce values
topics.summary: Recognise an expression as something that evaluates to a value, evaluate it using variables' current values, and use expressions directly as print arguments.

knowledge_points.title: print(2 + 3) vs print("2 + 3")
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(2 + 3)     # 5
print("2 + 3")   # 2 + 3
Without quotes Python evaluates the expression; with quotes it is text.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output for quoted and unquoted look-alikes.

knowledge_points.title: Expressions use the variables' current values
knowledge_points.practice: Evaluate expressions given variable values; trace values across reassignments.

knowledge_points.title: A bare expression line computes but shows nothing in a script
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 4
x * 2          # evaluated, then discarded
print(x * 2)   # 8
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output of scripts mixing bare expressions and prints; fix a script that prints nothing.

knowledge_points.title: Expressions as arguments
knowledge_points.worked_example:
price = 4
qty = 3
print("Total:", price * qty)
# Total: 12
knowledge_points.practice: Write one print that shows a label and a computed value.

topics.title: Order of operations
topics.summary: Predict the value of mixed expressions using Python's precedence rules (** first, then * / // %, then + -, left to right) and add parentheses to change or clarify the order.

knowledge_points.title: * and / before + and -
knowledge_points.practice: Evaluate expressions step by step; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: Parentheses go first
knowledge_points.practice: Add parentheses so an expression gives a target value.

knowledge_points.title: Same level: left to right; // and % share * and /'s level
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of chains of same-level operators.

knowledge_points.title: ** binds tightest, even tighter than a leading minus
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(-2 ** 2)     # -4, i.e. -(2 ** 2)
print((-2) ** 2)   # 4
print(2 ** 3 ** 2)  # 512: ** groups right to left
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results with unary minus and stacked powers.

topics.title: Turning formulas into Python
topics.summary: Translate everyday and maths formulas into correct Python expressions, using parentheses and intermediate variables to avoid precedence bugs. (Project-shaped: pairs well with a multistep exercise.)

knowledge_points.title: The average bug: a + b / 2
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = 4
b = 8
print(a + b / 2)     # 8.0  wrong
print((a + b) / 2)   # 6.0  right
knowledge_points.practice: Fix formulas missing parentheses; predict both versions.

knowledge_points.title: Temperature conversion
knowledge_points.practice: Write Python for given formulas (Celsius to Fahrenheit, km to miles).

knowledge_points.title: Formulas with powers
knowledge_points.practice: Write compound-growth and area/volume formulas; predict values.

knowledge_points.title: Break a long formula into named steps
knowledge_points.worked_example:
subtotal = price * qty
tax = subtotal * 0.08
total = subtotal + tax
Each line is easy to check on its own.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a one-line formula as named steps (Parsons); fill in a missing step.

topics.title: Named constants instead of magic numbers
topics.summary: Give fixed values UPPER_CASE names, use them in place of unexplained numbers, and know Python treats this as a convention rather than a rule.

knowledge_points.title: UPPER_CASE names for values that never change
knowledge_points.worked_example:
TAX_RATE = 0.08
price = 50
print(price * TAX_RATE)   # 4.0
knowledge_points.practice: Pick which names follow the constant convention; write a constant and use it.

knowledge_points.title: Replacing magic numbers
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(3 * 7 * 24)
DAYS_PER_WEEK = 7
HOURS_PER_DAY = 24
print(3 * DAYS_PER_WEEK * HOURS_PER_DAY)
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a short program replacing magic numbers with constants.

knowledge_points.title: Change it in one place
knowledge_points.worked_example: If the tax rate changes, edit only TAX_RATE = 0.10; every use updates.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a program where a hard-coded rate was updated in one place but not another.

knowledge_points.title: Python does not enforce constants
knowledge_points.worked_example:
MAX_SPEED = 120
MAX_SPEED = 200   # allowed, but breaks the promise
print(MAX_SPEED)  # 200
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output when a constant is reassigned; multiple choice on what UPPER_CASE signals.

topics.title: None: the value that means 'nothing yet'
topics.summary: Use None as a placeholder value, tell it apart from 0, "" and "None", and recognise the TypeError from doing arithmetic on a value that is still None.

knowledge_points.title: None is a value of its own type
knowledge_points.worked_example:
result = None
print(result)         # None
print(type(result))   # <class 'NoneType'>
knowledge_points.practice: Predict print() and type() output for None.

knowledge_points.title: None is not 0, not "" and not "None"
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(type(0), type(""), type("None"), type(None))
# int, str, str, NoneType
knowledge_points.practice: Classify look-alike values by type; multiple choice on which means 'no value'.

knowledge_points.title: A placeholder until the real value is known
knowledge_points.worked_example:
best_score = None
# ... later ...
best_score = 42
print(best_score)   # 42
knowledge_points.practice: Trace a variable that starts as None and is later assigned.

knowledge_points.title: Using None as if it were a number fails
knowledge_points.worked_example:
total = None
print(total + 1)
# TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'NoneType' and 'int'
knowledge_points.practice: Find why a program raises TypeError mentioning NoneType and fix the initial value.

topics.title: Checking for None with is
topics.summary: Test for None with is None / is not None, use == (not is) for numbers and strings, and distinguish 'is None' from 'is falsy'.

knowledge_points.title: x is None and x is not None
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = None
print(x is None)       # True
print(x is not None)   # False
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of is None checks after assignments.

knowledge_points.title: Why is, not ==, for None
knowledge_points.worked_example: is asks 'is this the very same object?'. There is only one None, so x is None is exact and is the PEP 8 style.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the idiomatic check among options; rewrite == None checks.

knowledge_points.title: Use == for numbers and strings, never is
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 5
print(x == 5)   # True
print(x is 5)   # Python warns: "is" with a literal, did you mean "=="?
knowledge_points.practice: Fix comparisons that misuse is; predict which lines produce a warning.

knowledge_points.title: None is falsy, but so is 0
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 0
print(not x)       # True
print(x is None)   # False
Only is None tells 'no value' apart from a real 0.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict not x vs x is None for 0, "", None and 5.

topics.title: Converting strings to numbers with int() and float()
topics.summary: Turn numeric text into int or float values so arithmetic works, and predict which strings raise ValueError.

knowledge_points.title: int("42") and float("3.5")
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = int("42")
print(n + 1)          # 43
print(float("3.5") * 2)   # 7.0
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of conversions followed by arithmetic.

knowledge_points.title: Fixing "5" + 3
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("5" + 3)        # TypeError
print(int("5") + 3)   # 8
knowledge_points.practice: Fix TypeErrors from mixing strings and numbers by converting the string.

knowledge_points.title: Spaces are fine; other characters are a ValueError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(int(" 7 "))      # 7
int("7 apples")
# ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10
knowledge_points.practice: For each string decide: converts (to what) or ValueError.

knowledge_points.title: int("3.5") fails: decimals need float()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
int("3.5")          # ValueError
float("3.5")        # 3.5
int(float("3.5"))   # 3
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the right conversion for each string; fix a crashing conversion.

topics.title: Converting between numbers and to text
topics.summary: Use str() to turn numbers into text, int() to truncate floats (toward zero) and float() to widen ints, and choose between int() and round().

knowledge_points.title: str() turns a number into text
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = str(42)
print(type(s))   # <class 'str'>
print(str(3.5)) # 3.5
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the type and value of str() results.

knowledge_points.title: int() of a float chops off the decimals, toward zero
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(int(3.9))    # 3
print(int(-3.9))   # -3
knowledge_points.practice: Predict int() of positive and negative floats.

knowledge_points.title: int() truncates, round() rounds
knowledge_points.worked_example: print(int(3.9), round(3.9))   # 3 4
knowledge_points.practice: Choose int() or round() for a described goal; fix a program that should round but truncates.

knowledge_points.title: float() widens an int
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(float(3))   # 3.0
print(float("7")) # 7.0
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the conversion that produces a target value and type from a given one.

topics.title: Reading text from the user with input()
topics.summary: Ask the user a question with input("prompt"), store the answer in a variable and use it, predicting output for given typed responses.

knowledge_points.title: input() waits and returns what the user typed
knowledge_points.worked_example:
name = input()
print("Hi", name)
# user types: Ada
# Hi Ada
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output for a given typed response.

knowledge_points.title: A prompt tells the user what to type
knowledge_points.worked_example:
name = input("Your name: ")
The prompt is shown, not stored. Without the trailing space the answer is jammed against the colon.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the exact screen transcript including the prompt; fix a prompt missing its space.

knowledge_points.title: Several inputs, read in order
knowledge_points.worked_example:
first = input("First: ")
last = input("Last: ")
print(last, first)
# user types Ada, then Lovelace -> Lovelace Ada
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output for two or three inputs; reorder lines (Parsons) to ask then print.

knowledge_points.title: Bugs: answer not stored, or quotes around the name
knowledge_points.worked_example:
input("Name: ")
print(name)        # NameError: the answer was never stored
print("name")      # prints the word name
knowledge_points.practice: Fix input programs that lose the answer or print the wrong thing.

topics.title: Reading numbers from the user
topics.summary: Convert input() results with int() or float() before doing arithmetic, and recognise the bugs when you forget ("3" + "4" gives 34) or pick the wrong conversion.

knowledge_points.title: input() always returns a string
knowledge_points.worked_example:
age = input("Age: ")
print(type(age))
# user types: 30
# <class 'str'>
knowledge_points.practice: Predict type() of input results for numeric-looking answers.

knowledge_points.title: Convert right away: int(input(...))
knowledge_points.worked_example:
age = int(input("Age: "))
print(age + 1)
# user types: 30 -> 31
knowledge_points.practice: Write the line that reads a whole number; predict output for typed values.

knowledge_points.title: Forgetting to convert: "3" + "4" is 34
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = input()
b = input()
print(a + b)
# user types 3, then 4 -> 34
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output of unconverted input arithmetic; fix it.

knowledge_points.title: float() for decimals; int() fails on "2.5"
knowledge_points.worked_example:
price = float(input("Price: "))
# user types 2.5 -> 2.5
int(input()) with 2.5 typed raises ValueError.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose int or float for each prompt; predict which typed answers crash.

topics.title: Input, compute, output: small console programs
topics.summary: Write short programs that read values, compute a result with a formula, and print it, such as a tip calculator or unit converter. (Project-shaped: a natural multistep.)

knowledge_points.title: Read one number, compute, print
knowledge_points.worked_example:
c = float(input("Celsius: "))
f = c * 9 / 5 + 32
print("Fahrenheit:", f)
# user types 100 -> Fahrenheit: 212.0
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output for a typed value; write a converter for a given formula.

knowledge_points.title: Two inputs combined
knowledge_points.worked_example:
bill = float(input("Bill: "))
pct = int(input("Tip %: "))
print("Tip:", round(bill * pct / 100, 2))
knowledge_points.practice: Write a program combining two inputs (area, tip, average); test it with given inputs.

knowledge_points.title: Putting the steps in order
knowledge_points.worked_example: Read -> convert -> compute -> print. Computing before reading is a NameError.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder a scrambled program (Parsons); fix one that computes before reading.

topics.title: True and False
topics.summary: Use the bool values True and False, store them in descriptively named variables, and avoid the 'true' and "True" look-alikes.

knowledge_points.title: True and False are values of type bool
knowledge_points.worked_example:
is_raining = True
print(is_raining)         # True
print(type(is_raining))   # <class 'bool'>
knowledge_points.practice: Predict print and type() output for bool variables.

knowledge_points.title: Capital T and F; no quotes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = true      # NameError: Python sees an unknown name
y = "True"    # a str, not a bool
z = True      # a bool
knowledge_points.practice: Classify look-alikes as bool, str or error; fix them.

knowledge_points.title: Name booleans as yes/no questions
knowledge_points.worked_example:
is_logged_in = False
has_ticket = True
Names like is_/has_ read naturally later in conditions.
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the best bool name; write two flag variables for a described situation.

topics.title: Truthy and falsy values
topics.summary: Predict bool() of numbers, strings and None (0, 0.0, "" and None are False; everything else here is True) and use True/False as 1/0 in arithmetic.

knowledge_points.title: Numbers: zero is False, everything else True
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(bool(0), bool(0.0))   # False False
print(bool(7), bool(-1))    # True True
knowledge_points.practice: Predict bool() of several numbers.

knowledge_points.title: Strings: only the empty string is False
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(bool(""))        # False
print(bool(" "))       # True (a space)
print(bool("False"))   # True (non-empty text)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict bool() of strings including tricky ones.

knowledge_points.title: None is False
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(bool(None))   # False
Falsy so far: False, 0, 0.0, "", None.
knowledge_points.practice: Sort a list of values into truthy and falsy.

knowledge_points.title: True and False count as 1 and 0
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(True + True)   # 2
print(False * 10)    # 0
knowledge_points.practice: Predict arithmetic on bools.

topics.title: Comparing numbers: < > <= >= == !=
topics.summary: Write comparisons that evaluate to True or False, use == (not =) for equality, and store comparison results in bool variables.

knowledge_points.title: < > <= >= produce True or False
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(3 < 5)    # True
print(5 <= 5)   # True
print(7 > 9)    # False
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of comparisons, especially the <= / < boundary.

knowledge_points.title: == tests equality; = assigns
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 4         # assignment
print(x == 4) # True
print(x = 4)  # TypeError: inside print, x = 4 is read as a keyword argument
knowledge_points.practice: Fix comparisons written with =; multiple choice between = and ==.

knowledge_points.title: != means not equal
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(3 != 4)   # True
print(4 != 4)   # False
knowledge_points.practice: Predict != results; rewrite a described condition using != or ==.

knowledge_points.title: Comparing expressions and storing the result
knowledge_points.worked_example:
age = 20
is_adult = age >= 18
is_even = age % 2 == 0
print(is_adult, is_even)   # True True
knowledge_points.practice: Write bool variables for described conditions (even, positive, over limit).

topics.title: Comparing across types and comparing strings
topics.summary: Predict comparisons between ints and floats, strings and numbers, and strings with each other (exact, case-sensitive, ordered character by character).

knowledge_points.title: int vs float compare by value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(3 == 3.0)   # True
print(2 < 2.5)    # True
knowledge_points.practice: Predict mixed int/float comparisons.

knowledge_points.title: A string never equals a number; ordering them is a TypeError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("3" == 3)   # False
print("3" < 4)
# TypeError: '<' not supported between 'str' and 'int'
knowledge_points.practice: For each comparison give True, False or TypeError; fix with int().

knowledge_points.title: String equality is exact
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("yes" == "yes")   # True
print("yes" == "Yes")   # False
print("yes" == "yes ")  # False: trailing space
knowledge_points.practice: Predict equality of strings differing in case or spacing.

knowledge_points.title: String ordering goes character by character
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("apple" < "banana")   # True
print("Zoo" < "apple")     # True: capitals sort first
print("10" < "9")          # True: compares '1' with '9'
knowledge_points.practice: Predict string orderings, including digits-as-text and capitals.

topics.title: Range checks and comparing floats
topics.summary: Write chained range checks such as 0 <= x < 10 with the right inclusive/exclusive bounds, and compare floats with a tolerance instead of ==.

knowledge_points.title: Chained comparisons
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 7
print(0 < x < 10)   # True
It means 0 < x and x < 10.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict chained comparisons for several x values.

knowledge_points.title: Inclusive or exclusive bounds
knowledge_points.worked_example:
score = 100
print(0 <= score <= 100)   # True
print(0 <= score < 100)    # False: 100 is excluded
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the right bounds for a described range; fix an off-by-one boundary.

knowledge_points.title: == on floats can surprise
knowledge_points.practice: Predict float equality results.

knowledge_points.title: Compare floats with a tolerance
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = 0.1 + 0.2
print(abs(a - 0.3) < 1e-9)   # True
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite float == checks using abs(a - b) < tolerance.

topics.title: Combining conditions with and, or, not
topics.summary: Evaluate and, or and not on True/False and use them to combine comparisons.

knowledge_points.title: and: True only if both sides are True
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(True and True)    # True
print(True and False)   # False
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the truth table for and; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: or: True if at least one side is True
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(False or True)    # True
print(False or False)   # False
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the truth table for or; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: not flips a bool
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(not True)       # False
print(not (3 > 5))    # True
knowledge_points.practice: Predict not applied to bools and comparisons.

knowledge_points.title: Combining comparisons
knowledge_points.worked_example:
age = 15
is_teen = age >= 13 and age <= 19
print(is_teen)   # True
knowledge_points.practice: Write bool expressions for described rules (teen, weekend, free ticket).

topics.title: Precedence and common mistakes with and/or
topics.summary: Predict expressions mixing not, and, or by precedence, add parentheses for intended meaning, and avoid the x == 1 or 2 bug.

knowledge_points.title: not, then and, then or
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(True or False and False)    # True: and goes first
print((True or False) and False)  # False
knowledge_points.practice: Predict mixed expressions; add parentheses to match a stated meaning.

knowledge_points.title: Outside a range: or, not and
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 120
print(x < 0 or x > 100)   # True
x < 0 and x > 100 can never be True.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose and or or for described conditions; fix an impossible condition.

knowledge_points.title: The x == 1 or 2 bug
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 5
print(x == 1 or 2)        # 2 (truthy!), not False
print(x == 1 or x == 2)   # False
Each side of or is a separate condition.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix conditions that compare against several values; predict the buggy version's result.

topics.title: Negating conditions (De Morgan's laws)
topics.summary: Rewrite the negation of a combined condition: not (a and b) is (not a) or (not b), and simplify not around comparisons.

knowledge_points.title: not around a comparison flips the operator
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 3
print(not x > 5)   # True
print(x <= 5)      # True: the same check
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite not-comparisons without not.

knowledge_points.title: not (a and b) == (not a) or (not b)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a, b = True, False
print(not (a and b))       # True
print((not a) or (not b))  # True
knowledge_points.practice: Check equivalence with a truth table; choose the correct rewrite.

knowledge_points.title: not (a or b) == (not a) and (not b)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 50
print(not (x < 0 or x > 100))   # True
print(x >= 0 and x <= 100)      # True
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite negated range checks; fix a negation that only flipped the operators.

topics.title: Short-circuit evaluation
topics.summary: Predict when and/or stop early, use that to guard risky expressions such as division, and understand that and/or return one of their operands.

knowledge_points.title: and stops at the first False
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 0
print(x != 0 and 10 / x > 1)   # False, no error
The right side never runs when the left is False.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether a guarded expression errors or gives a value.

knowledge_points.title: Order matters: put the guard first
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 0
print(10 / x > 1 and x != 0)
# ZeroDivisionError: the risky part ran first
knowledge_points.practice: Fix expressions whose guard is on the wrong side.

knowledge_points.title: or stops at the first True
knowledge_points.worked_example: print(True or 1 / 0)   # True, no error
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which expressions short-circuit and which raise errors.

knowledge_points.title: and/or return an operand, not always a bool
knowledge_points.worked_example:
name = ""
print(name or "guest")   # guest
print(0 and 5)           # 0
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the value of and/or on non-bool operands; write a default-value expression.
